title: How I got highlighted by OpenAI in their pretraining competition
description: CaseOps, phased test-time training, and making the most of 16 MB.
markdown:
OpenAI [highlighted my CaseOps tokenizer](https://openai.com/index/what-parameter-golf-taught-us/) in its Parameter Golf write-up, in the section on new modeling and data ideas. The idea was small: stop making a tiny language model learn separate vocabulary for the same word in different cases.

The other contribution I want to talk about is phased test-time training. It lets the model carry something useful from one evaluation document into the next.

These were the two most interesting things I contributed to the competition. One changes how text is represented. The other changes when the model gets to learn.

## A language model in 16 MB

[Parameter Golf](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf) asked us to train the best language model we could fit into a 16 MB artifact, including the counted code and compressed weights. Training had to finish within ten minutes on eight H100s. Evaluation got its own ten-minute budget.

The score was bits per byte on held-out FineWeb text. Lower is better: how many bits does the model need, on average, to encode a byte of the original text?

That makes tokenization unusually interesting. You can change the vocabulary or the representation, but you still pay for predicting the same original text. Under a small memory budget, the question becomes how much of the model's capacity is going toward useful distinctions.

## CaseOps

Consider these:

```text
apple
Apple
APPLE
```

They share almost all their structure. A conventional case-sensitive vocabulary can spend separate entries on those variants, or break them into different subword sequences. Either way, capitalization gets tangled up with the lexical representation.

CaseOps separates the two. The lexical stream is lowercase; a small set of operators preserves the casing.

```text
apple  → apple
Apple  → [TITLE]apple
APPLE  → [ALLCAPS]apple
```

Now the tokenizer can reuse the same lowercase pieces, while the model learns a reusable capitalization operation.

This is a reversible transform before SentencePiece BPE. The representation still contains every capital letter. The model has to predict the operators too.

### Four small operators

The [implementation](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/blob/main/records/track_10min_16mb/2026-04-18_PR1626_CaseOps_Taper/lossless_caps.py) works over runs of ASCII letters:

- **TITLE** capitalizes the first letter of a run.
- **ALLCAPS** capitalizes the whole run.
- **CAPNEXT** capitalizes the next letter, for mixed-case words.
- **ESC** escapes a literal control character.

Lowercase runs pass through unchanged. Non-ASCII characters also pass through unchanged. The operators are reserved characters in the actual transform; the names below make them readable.

<!--CASEOPS_DEMO-->

Mixed case makes the benefit a little less tidy. A name like OpenAI needs multiple operations. But title case and all-caps words have short descriptions, and the transform gives us those descriptions directly.

The useful bias is that spelling and casing can share structure. Learning what “apple” means no longer has to be completely separate from learning how to capitalize it. With only 8,192 vocabulary entries, that is an appealing place to save duplication.

### Counting the original bytes

There is one important bookkeeping detail. The transformed stream has a different byte length, so scoring against its bytes would change the task.

The exporter writes a byte-count sidecar alongside the validation tokens. The evaluator uses those counts to charge the prediction loss against the **original UTF-8 bytes**. Capitalization operators still cost prediction bits; inserting them doesn't inflate the denominator.

```math
\mathrm{BPB}=\frac{\text{total negative log-likelihood in nats}}
{\ln(2)\times\text{original byte count}}.
```

The [exporter and record README](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/tree/main/records/track_10min_16mb/2026-04-18_PR1626_CaseOps_Taper) have the transform, reserved-symbol configuration, and byte-accounting details.

My [CaseOps submission](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1729) finished at **1.06780 BPB** averaged over three seeds, in about **15.94 MB**. It combined the tokenizer with a mild late weight-decay taper on the existing phased-TTT stack. That number belongs to the whole submission.

What I like about CaseOps is how little machinery it needs. The transformer stays a transformer. We just give it a representation with less duplicated structure to learn.

## Phased test-time training

The competition allowed a useful form of online learning: once a token had been scored, the model could train on it to help predict future tokens. Its original score stayed fixed.

Earlier work by [samacqua](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1530) already used this inside each document. Score a chunk, update a LoRA adapter using that chunk, then predict the next one. At the document boundary, reset the adapter.

That gives the model a short-lived memory of the current document. My addition was to let the shared base model learn across documents as well.

### Two timescales

Document-local adaptation is good at picking up the topic, terminology, and style of the text you're currently reading. But resetting the adapter throws that adaptation away.

The base model offers a second place to put learning. It can absorb changes from already-scored documents and pass them on to later ones. Local LoRA still handles the specifics of each new document.

My [first phased implementation](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1610) kept the existing evaluator and inserted one pause:

1. Score documents using the usual per-document LoRA adaptation.
2. After 2,000 documents have completed in the evaluation queue, gather those documents.
3. Run distributed SGD on that already-scored prefix to update the base model.
4. Resume the queue with the updated base and fresh local adapters for subsequent documents.

<!--TTT_DIAGRAM-->

The ordering is the whole trick. The global update only sees documents whose scores are already counted. It improves the starting point for later predictions without going back and changing earlier scores.

### Why phases

I initially tried a more continuous combination of local and global updates. It was harder to make that run efficiently across GPUs: synchronizing the shared base model kept getting in the way of the local work.

A phase boundary makes that coordination much simpler. The GPUs finish a defined amount of scoring, do a shared training job, then return to scoring. It also makes the information flow easy to follow: everything entering global SGD has already been evaluated.

The [original record](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/blob/main/records/track_10min_16mb/2026-04-13_VarLenAttn_PhasingTTT2000/README.md) left training unchanged and moved the three-seed mean from **1.07336388 to 1.07280628 BPB**, with evaluation taking about 507 seconds on average. A small improvement, with an extra learning mechanism that others could build on.

And they did. [dexhunter's next version](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1626) extended the idea to three phases, alternating scoring and global SGD several times. That was the stack I later built the CaseOps submission on.

I like that loop: contribute an idea, someone improves it, then their improvement becomes the starting point for your next experiment.

## Sharing what can be shared

CaseOps and phased TTT solve different problems, but both make better use of shared structure.

CaseOps shares lexical pieces across capitalization patterns. Phased TTT shares learning across documents while preserving a separate, fast adaptation path for each one.

The constraints made both ideas worth trying. With a much larger model or a much longer run, it is easy to leave a bit of duplication or unused learning on the table. Sixteen megabytes and a ten-minute clock make you notice it.

And sometimes a few capitalization operators are enough to get your tokenizer into OpenAI's write-up.

title: Reverse engineering DiMuon through a training API
description: A hidden optimizer, a programmable LoRA adapter, and a symmetry trick that made the update rule fall out.
markdown:
Thinking Machines released DiMuon, a LoRA optimizer available through [Tinker](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/tinker/optimizers/), without publishing its update equations. We tried to recover them using only the API.

We ended up with a local reconstruction that replayed **four batches of SST2 gradients with every recovered FP16 polar-output value matching**. That experiment used rank-one LoRA on Qwen3-8B's output projection, with gradients measured at Tinker's weights.

The fun parts were finding the rule, making the API reveal it, and then chasing the rounding that gave the implementation away.

## The rule: scale, polar, scale again

[Muon](https://kellerjordan.github.io/posts/muon/) takes a momentum matrix and approximately makes its nonzero singular values equal. This stops the largest singular direction from dominating the update.

The interesting addition in DiMuon is a **row-and-column sandwich**. The previous momentum determines which rows and columns to scale. Apply that scaling before Muon's polar transform, then apply it again afterward.

<!--DIMUON_SANDWICH-->

Rows and columns with stronger old momentum get smaller multipliers. The two LoRA matrices—the wide A and tall B—get the same final update norm.

It's a compact way to adapt Muon's geometry to the coordinates of each factor. The statistics are cheap to compute, and the momentum already contains the history they need.

## The trick: turn the model into a linear system

LoRA learns a weight change **BA**: A compresses an input into a few coordinates, and B expands it back out. The original model weight stays frozen.

At initialization, **B = 0**. Put that adapter on the output projection, and the transformer supplies a fixed feature h. The trainable addition to the logits is just sBAh. From B's perspective, an eight-billion-parameter language model has become a linear system.

We could simplify the loss too. Cross-entropy contains a shared log-sum-exp term; signed token weights that sum to zero cancel it. What's left is a linear combination of logits.

Now we could construct useful gradient patterns instead of hoping ordinary text would produce them. To read those gradients back, we borrowed [Martin Marek's large-epsilon Adam trick](https://x.com/mrtnm/status/2114145574987702525): choose an invertible optimizer step, download the weights, and undo the step mathematically. Adam became our gradient meter.

## The best experiment: make the unknown cancel

We wanted to know whether DiMuon scaled the matrix **after** the polar transform. But we hadn't reproduced that transform precisely yet.

So we chose a gradient that made two axes equal at its input. Symmetry forces the polar computation to treat them equally. Their common response cancels when you take the output ratio—leaving the post-scaling exposed.

<!--DIMUON_ISOLATION-->

That ratio agreed to about eight significant figures. We could identify the machinery around an operation without knowing exactly how the operation was implemented.

A second simple experiment explained where the scaling came from: build history with learning rate zero, then set beta to zero for the measured step. The current momentum forgets the past, yet the update still changes. The old momentum is doing a second job: choosing the row and column scaling.

## Same math, different program

The numerics turned into a second puzzle: **which way of computing the same equation matched the API?** Three details stood out.

### Rearrange the polynomial

Each polar stage applies a polynomial to the working matrix X. Here R = XᵀX, I is the identity, and a, b, c are that stage's coefficients. We initially evaluated it in expanded form. The breakthrough was switching to **Horner form**:

<!--DIMUON_HORNER-->

The coefficients stayed the same. The rearranged version matched all eleven of our retained numerical fingerprints.

This is a natural optimization for LoRA: X is tall and skinny, while R is only rank × rank. Folding the aX term into the small matrix avoids a separate multiply-and-add over the entire large matrix. It also changes where rounding happens. The algebra alone doesn't tell you which program ran.

### Catch an intermediate being rounded

Inside the Horner calculation, **cR gets rounded to FP16 before adding bI**. Keeping that intermediate in higher precision gives a different answer.

We made two inputs specifically to distinguish those implementations. Skipping the FP16 store missed their tiny output ratios by about **20% and 4.6%**; including it matched both to roughly **4 × 10⁻⁸** relative error.

That's a surprisingly specific thing to learn through an API. A low-precision tensor operation naturally leaves this kind of trace: the result gets stored before the next operation reads it. “More accurate” arithmetic erased the trace we were trying to reproduce.

### Let the GPU split up the work

One CPU replay still differed by **0.79%**. Native FP16 matrix products on an H100 brought that case to roughly **8 × 10⁻⁸**. The first Gram matrix differed by just one FP16 rounding step; the polynomial amplified it.

Profiling our GPU replay exposed a useful reason: **split-K**. The GPU divides a long dot product into chunks, computes them in parallel, then combines the partial sums. That helps keep it busy when the output matrix is tiny—exactly the shape LoRA produces. [cuBLAS allows those partial sums to be stored in FP16](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/12.8.0/cublas/index.html#cublasltreduction-scheme-t), adding another rounding boundary.

We could reproduce two of our GPU execution paths by changing only the split count and partial-sum precision. The interesting part was that an ordinary parallelization choice left a visible signature in the optimizer's output.

That's what I liked about this project: the breakthroughs came from making the system answer a smaller question. Freeze one factor. Cancel a term in the loss. Make two axes equal. Each simplification removed something we otherwise would have had to guess.

notes:
These are the equations and measurement details behind [Reverse engineering DiMuon through a training API](/reverse-engineering-dimuon/).

## The gradient-meter equations

With no clipping or weight decay, a coordinate moves by:

```math
u=-\eta\frac{g}{|g|+\epsilon},
\qquad
g=-\frac{\epsilon u}{\eta-|u|}.
```

Large epsilon avoids saturation. We repeated measurements with different epsilon values to check the recovered gradients, including their rounding.

## The complete update equations

After optional joint gradient clipping, form the current momentum:

```math
M_t=\beta M_{t-1}+(1-\beta)\widetilde G_t.
```

Compute energies from the previous momentum:

```math
e_i=\sum_j M_{t-1,ij}^2,
\qquad f_j=\sum_i M_{t-1,ij}^2.
```

Normalize each vector by its maximum, add a small ridge, and take the inverse fourth root:

```math
D_r=\operatorname{diag}\left[\left(\frac{e_i}{\max_k e_k}+10^{-4}\right)^{-1/4}\right],
```

```math
D_c=\operatorname{diag}\left[\left(\frac{f_j}{\max_k f_k}+10^{-4}\right)^{-1/4}\right].
```

Zero old momentum uses relative energies of one. The ridge keeps inactive coordinates from getting unbounded multipliers. Energy is a squared norm, so its inverse fourth root is an inverse square root of the norm.

Then:

```math
U_t=D_r\,\Phi(D_rM_tD_c)\,D_c,
\qquad \Delta\theta_t=-\eta C(r)\frac{U_t}{\|U_t\|_F}.
```

Φ includes the approximate polar computation and its input normalization. A zero direction gets a zero update. At alpha 32, tested ranks 1 through 64 followed:

```math
C(r)=\sqrt r\left(\frac r{32}\right)^{0.175}.
```

This predicted a held-out rank-16 norm to about 5.6 × 10⁻⁸ relative error. The origin of 0.175 is still a mystery.

## The polar computation we replayed

Normalize the preconditioned momentum and store it in FP16:

```math
X=\operatorname{round}_{\mathrm{FP16}}\left(
\frac{D_rM_tD_c}{1.01\max(\|D_rM_tD_c\|_F,10^{-7})}
\right).
```

For a tall matrix, form the small Gram matrix R = XᵀX and apply a stage:

```math
X\leftarrow X\left[aI+R(bI+cR)\right].
```

The coefficients change each stage. Wide matrices use the transposed construction. The intermediate stores matter, as does how the GPU reduces each matrix product.

## Experiment and measurement details

The ordinary steps use learning rate 0.001. Subtracting two nearly equal exported weights loses precision, so we also measure updates with the learning rate enlarged to 16. That changes the readout gain while keeping the optimizer state and gradient fixed.

With that readout, relative update errors were 7.6 × 10⁻⁸ to 1.21 × 10⁻⁷. At the ordinary learning rate, errors in the subtracted updates range from roughly 2 × 10⁻⁶ to 2.4 × 10⁻⁵; the accumulated local weights differ from the hosted weights by at most 9.3 × 10⁻¹⁰. The replay uses measured gradients at the hosted weights; it does not recompute them with a separate local language model. Other experiments include an unresolved 0.81% discrepancy in a rank-two B continuation and 1.14% RMS across historical A updates. The [replay data](/data/dimuon-replay-2026-10-31.json) covers the four-step rank-one experiment.
